newsitem.title: UK: Former UK premier Heath says Clarke will not quit.
newsitem.headline: Former UK premier Heath says Clarke will not quit.

text.p: Former British prime minister Edward Heath said on Tuesday he was confident Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke would not leave the government in a row over whether Britain would join a single European currency.

Asked whether he agreed with Home Secretary Michael Howard speaking earlier on the BBC that there was an agreed policy on a single currency in the cabinet, Heath said: "I can't answer for the members of the cabinet."
He said the latest row had been caused by anti-Europeans in the party who wanted to stampede the government into ruling out a single currency before the general election.
But Heath said: "He (Clarke) won't leave the government." Asked whether he was confident of this, he said: "Quite confident, because he knows he's done a splendid job and he will keep on doing it."

Major has been trying to contain divisions in his party over Europe, but remarks by Clarke over the weekend that Britain could lose its opportunity of joining a European single currency if it "dithered" about entering at the start ropened the rifts.

Newspapers, quoting colleagues of the prime minister, reported on Tuesday that Major was "very angry" at Clarke's remarks, which officials in Major's Downing Street office pointedly declined to endorse.
Clarke's remarks, his most forthright on a single currency, come after senior Conservative figures last week began a fightback against the anti-Europeans in the party.
Anti-Europeans would dearly love to remove Clarke, the most forthrightly pro-European member of the cabinet. But Major's hands are tied as markets would be dismayed by such a move.

Howard, on the "Eurosceptic" wing of the party, tried to paper over the rift on Tuesday, saying the government continued to retain its opt out on the single currency negotiated by Prime Minister John Major at Maastricht.
Howard said the ruling party's position was clear in contrast to the opposition. "We will resist any further moves down the road to a federal Europe," Howard told the BBC.
